transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-06
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Vale (Hawthorne - Dir Platform), Sana Ortiz (Hawthorne - Cloud Sec), Eli Chen (Hawthorne - Compliance)

Auto-summary: Quick run through of private/VPC/on-prem topology patterns. Focus on enforcing outbound egress allowlist, preventing accidental leak to public endpoints, integrating customer KMS/HSM, and RBAC + SSO mapping for operators. Discussed SOC 2 artifacts and audit log retention windows.

[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone thanks for jumping on, I see we have Marcus, Sana, Eli, and my colleague Priya. we'll tee up the runbook and walk through options for air-gapping and egress control, is that the right goal for today?
[00:18] Marcus Vale: yeah that's right. our risk team asked specifically for patterns where the inference cluster is effectively air-gapped except for a small set of monitored egress flows, and they want to understand how Redwood's private control plane fits in with our network posture.
[00:31] Priya Nair: quick clarify — when you say air-gapped, do you mean completely no internet access from the serving nodes, or a restricted allowlist egress to things like our internal model registry and KMS?
[00:45] Sana Ortiz: restricted allowlist. we need to be able to pull models from our internal artifactory and to push logs to our splunk, but nothing else. zero direct outbound to the general internet.
[00:58] Eli Chen: also SOC2 folks want proof of deterministic egress: where every external flow is logged and approved. retention for those logs is 7 years for certain artifacts so we need to make sure the platform can hand over audit logs in a compliant format.
[01:16] Jordan Lee: understood. Priya i'll start with the high-level topology options we typically recommend for Private/VPC deployments.
[01:24] Priya Nair: cool, so option A is fully air-gapped on-prem with an isolated control plane — that means the Redwood control plane runs in your environment and the serving nodes have no direct internet egress. the control plane manages the model orchestrations and we only allow outbound to your internal monitoring/KMS endpoints via a NAT/proxy.
[01:46] Priya Nair: option B is VPC with restricted egress and a peered management plane in our cloud — this reduces ops burden but you give us a small, audited egress path to Redwood-managed endpoints for metrics and updates. option C is a hybrid where the model artifacts live in your object store and the runtime pulls directly from there, while control plane interactions are tunneled through an approved proxy.
[02:09] Marcus Vale: hybrid sounds promising. are there transport-level guarantees for the tunnel? we can't have a persistent backchannel that could be used to exfiltrate data.
[02:21] Priya Nair: good question. the tunnel is mTLS only, uses mutual certs per cluster, and we support strict mTLS pinning and short-lived cert rotation. additionally we support idle timeouts and forced reauth every X minutes so the control plane can't stay connected forever without renewal.
[02:40] Sana Ortiz: can we run the control plane VM in our VPC and have it talk to Redwood for updates over an outbound TLS proxy we control?
[02:49] Jordan Lee: yep, that's the Private pattern many customers use. Redwood provides the control plane artifact, you run it in a private subnet. any outbound to Redwood endpoints is through your egress proxy and can be blocked except to a few pinned IPs or DNS entries.
[03:02] Jordan Lee: note that for SOC2 we typically hand over TLS termination certs, our audit logs, and a signed attestation. we'll share the PDF after the call.
[03:12] Eli Chen: great, we'll need the attestation plus a schema for the audit log export. can you also enumerate which events are logged? admin auth, model pulls, token redemptions, key accesses?
[03:26] Priya Nair: yes, event categories: admin auth (SSO/SAML assertions), role changes (RBAC), model artifact pulls, inference request metadata (no PII by default unless you send it), KMS key usage events, and egress decisions (allow/deny logs). we'll provide examples in JSONL format.
[03:47] Marcus Vale: on KMS: we use a managed HSM from vault-provider-x, with keys rotated quarterly via an internal operator. can Redwood integrate with an external KMS and not store plaintext keys?
[03:59] Priya Nair: Redwood's Private runtime supports customer-managed KMS/HSM. the runtime never persists plaintext material; it calls out to your KMS for signing/decrypt operations and caches only ephemeral tokens in memory. rotation is supported — we have a key id mapping and rotation hooks so you can rotate without downtime if you pre-stage keys.
[04:20] Sana Ortiz: how are those KMS calls routed? do they go out over the public internet or can they stay within our VPC to our internal vault?
[04:30] Priya Nair: they can stay on your internal network. we call the KMS endpoint you configure — either an internal VIP or an on-prem HSM appliance. if you use an external cloud KMS, calls go over mTLS through your egress proxy unless you allow a direct route.
[04:44] Jordan Lee: one practical detail — when customers use on-prem KMS, we recommend binding service accounts to machine identities and enforcing KMS policy at the HSM layer to prevent misuse.
[04:55] Eli Chen: fine. next, egress control specifics: what firewall/NACL rules do you require to prevent other outbound flows from the GNodes?
[05:07] Priya Nair: at minimum: block all outbound 0.0.0.0/0 except a tightly-scoped allowlist; allow DNS to a dedicated resolver in your VPC (or a resolution proxy); allow outbound to your log sink (e.g., Splunk/ELK) IPs; allow to your model registry or S3 endpoints; optionally allow to your KMS; and allow to Redwood control-plane IPs if you're using cloud-managed updates.
[05:34] Marcus Vale: we run a strict egress proxy that enforces HTTP allowlist and deep packet inspection. would Redwood be able to function through that? we can't loosen it.
[05:45] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood can operate behind an outbound proxy. we recommend configuring proxy authentication (mTLS or token) so the runtime can authenticate, and to allow CONNECT for our pinned endpoints. some features like auto-updates may need periodic whitelisting windows if the proxy blocks unknown certificate chains.
[06:05] Sana Ortiz: about audit logs: we need tamper-evident logs. do you support signed logs or syslog forwarding to our SIEM with proof-of-origin?
[06:15] Priya Nair: we support forwarders — syslog, JSONL over TLS to an endpoint, and S3-compatible sinks. for tamper-evidence we can provide signed attestations and append-only logs with HMAC chaining on request. not all customers enable that, but it's available.
[06:35] Jordan Lee: quick note on RBAC and SSO: how do you currently map IdP groups to Redwood roles?
[06:42] Priya Nair: we support SAML and OIDC for SSO. mapping from IdP groups to Redwood roles is via our role-mapping table in the control plane; we recommend least privilege: operators get deploy rights, auditors get read-only with log export, and devs get limited run access. you can sync groups periodically or via SCIM for automated provisioning.
[07:02] Marcus Vale: we use Okta and SCIM today. can we enforce step-up MFA for certain admin ops?
[07:09] Priya Nair: yes, that's handled at the IdP. Redwood honors the authentication context (ACR) from the IdP, so you can require higher assurance for role elevation or sensitive API calls.
[07:20] Eli Chen: what about secret zero and bootstrap — how do we initially provision the cluster so there's no human-exposed bootstrap key?
[07:28] Priya Nair: we provide a signed installation manifest that your infra engine (e.g., terraform) applies. the manifest contains ephemeral certs and a short-lived bootstrap token you redeem via a secure channel. after the initial handshake, tokens are rotated and the bootstrap token is revoked.
[07:44] Sana Ortiz: ok, good. let's talk about data residency — our models and logs for EU customers must stay in eu-west only. can you pin regions for Dedicated/Private?
[07:54] Jordan Lee: yes, Private deployments are fully yours; you can ensure objects and backups live in eu-west. For Dedicated, you can request regional placement. We'll include the data residency page in the docs we send.
[08:07] Marcus Vale: one of the harder asks is preventing accidental internet CVE callbacks from third-party libs in the runtime. do you support egress DNS interception or local blackhole routing?
[08:18] Priya Nair: we recommend two layers: (1) deny-all outbound and allow only the minimal list; (2) run a DNS proxy that resolves only approved names and returns NXDOMAIN for others. for defense-in-depth, a local eBPF-level egress filter could block sockets to non-authorized IP ranges. we have a reference IPTables/eBPF snippet we can share.
[08:41] Eli Chen: nice. on logging frequency and retention — we may need high-frequency request metadata for 90 days hot, then archive for 7 years. do you support tiered retention?
[08:52] Priya Nair: yes, logs can be tiered. hot storage in your splunk or our short-term store (if you opt in) and cold archives to S3 with lifecycle. we can produce signed manifests for long-term archive to satisfy auditors.
[09:10] Jordan Lee: let's pause for questions. Marcus?
[09:15] Marcus Vale: two quick ones — licensing: if we run Private on-prem, does Redwood still require a control-plane license fee? and network ops wants to know whether the runtime emits any heartbeats that reveal model names or tenant ids outside the VPC.
[09:31] Jordan Lee: licensing is a platform fee for Private + optional support tiers. we'll include options for perpetual+support and annual subscription. Regarding heartbeats, the runtime can be configured to emit only minimal health pings and all telemetry can be routed to your endpoints. model names/tenant ids are never leaked by default — only opaque cluster identifiers unless you opt into usage analytics.
[09:53] Sana Ortiz: Priya, can you walk through an example firewall rule set? high-level example like deny all, allow DNS, allow KMS, allow log sink with ports.
[10:03] Priya Nair: sure — example NACLs
  - 100: deny all outbound 0.0.0.0/0
  - 110: allow outbound TCP 53 to your resolver (or let's say TCP/UDP 53 if using normal DNS)
  - 120: allow outbound TCP 443 to splunk-ingest.example.internal (specific IPs)
  - 130: allow outbound to s3-vpc-endpoint IP range or your internal model registry (ports 443)
  - 140: allow outbound to KMS endpoint (port 443)
  - 150: allow to management proxy IPs for control-plane updates if you choose to use that flow
[10:36] Marcus Vale: for the s3 case, we prefer VPC Endpoints to avoid NAT. do you support signature v4 with those endpoints?
[10:44] Priya Nair: yes, we can authenticate to any S3-compatible endpoint using the credentials you provision. the runtime can be given an IAM role or static creds depending on your auth model. we prefer IRSA or roles for reduced key handling.
[10:56] Eli Chen: let's cover incident response — if there's a suspected exfil event, can we freeze the cluster or revoke network connectivity automatically from our side?
[11:05] Priya Nair: you should be able to — our runbook supports a freeze action which disables outgoing rules at the runtime level and revokes tokens. it's also possible to script network ACL changes from your firewall to isolate nodes. we can provide runbook playbooks for both scenarios.
[11:20] Jordan Lee: also we can ship a watch script that integrates with your SOAR to automate containment steps.
[11:28] Sana Ortiz: what about pentest/attestation schedules? auditors want to know if we can run our own pentest against the Private runtime.
[11:35] Priya Nair: you can — we have a coordinated disclosure process and a standard NDA & pentest engagement we sign. for SOC2 it's common to run annual pentests with agreed rules.
[11:46] Marcus Vale: good. something specific — our legal requires proof you don't persist customer PII in telemetry. does Redwood scrub requests before storing telemetry?
[11:57] Priya Nair: by default, we do not store input payloads in telemetry. there is an opt-in flag to keep traces for debugging, but it must be explicitly enabled per-tenant and we recommend tokenization. we also have redaction hooks to remove PII fields based on configured patterns.
[12:16] Eli Chen: any potential gotchas when using short-lived KV cache across restarts? i.e., if a node gets redeployed, could that cause replays to external endpoints?
[12:27] Priya Nair: KV cache is in memory; on restart it's rebuilt from the active session. we recommend sticky routing for inference sessions and persisting minimal session metadata to a private store if you want seamless failover. replays only happen if upstream clients resend requests; the runtime doesn't re-request external content except for model artifacts.
[12:45] Jordan Lee: we're about halfway through. quick sanity check on the items we'll share: network runbook, NACL/iptables snippets, SOC2 + ISO attestations, audit log schema, sample KMS integration guide, and a suggested PoC plan. sound right?
[12:58] Marcus Vale: yes.
[13:00] Sana Ortiz: yes please.
[13:02] Jordan Lee: ok let's dive into a quick PoC outline — week 0 is install & baseline, week 1 egress enforcement and KMS integration, week 2 load tests and telemetry validation, week 3 final handover and retention tests. Priya can be the SE lead on that.
[13:19] Priya Nair: I'll also run a short script to validate egress rules — basically test vectors that try to reach known-bad domains and ensure they're blocked, and verify allowed flows to KMS/logs/S3 succeed.
[13:31] Marcus Vale: perfect. 
[13:33] Eli Chen: I do have a compliance question about signed audit logs — is there a standard format you export for chain-of-custody?
[13:41] Priya Nair: we can export JSONL with SHA256 digests per-file and an overall signed manifest that includes each file's digest and timestamp. that satisfies many auditors; we also support WORM S3 endpoints if required.
[13:58] Sana Ortiz: about RBAC mapping — our IdP groups are fairly granular, but we want to avoid a 1:1 blow up. do you support role hierarchy or inheritance?
[14:09] Priya Nair: yes, Redwood roles support group mappings and hierarchical roles. you can map several IdP groups to a single Redwood role or nest roles. we recommend an audit sweep before cutover to flatten unnecessary groups.
[14:22] Jordan Lee: quick interruption — someone in the chat asked for a sample eBPF snippet. Priya can attach that after.
[14:29] Priya Nair: will do. I'll include an eBPF example and an IPTables fallback for teams that can't do eBPF yet.
[14:37] Marcus Vale: anything about network segmentation for multi-tenant clusters? we plan to run multiple business units in the same infra and need strict tenant boundaries.
[14:46] Priya Nair: we support both single-tenant cluster per BU and multi-tenant with strong namespace isolation. for multi-tenant we recommend network policies, per-namespace service accounts, and resource quotas. cryptographic separation is also possible by using per-tenant KMS keys.
[15:02] Eli Chen: ok. can we briefly cover evidence we need for our ISO audit? specifically: SSO setup docs, KMS integration validation, and proof of log retention policies.
[15:12] Jordan Lee: we'll provide a package: configuration snippets, screenshots of a live deployment (if you want), attestations, and a checklist of controls mapped to ISO clauses.
[15:23] Sana Ortiz: do you have templates for control mapping? that'd save us time.
[15:27] Priya Nair: yes — we'll send an ISO/SOC2 mapping spreadsheet that aligns Redwood controls to common frameworks.
[15:33] Marcus Vale: on metrics, we need to capture per-token latency and per-tenant cost breakdowns. can these be exported to our billing system?
[15:43] Priya Nair: yes, token-level metrics can be emitted and exported to your billing pipeline. we support CSV exports and direct integration with common billing bridges.
[15:52] Eli Chen: we've got to handle the case where a node accidentally has wider egress due to config drift. do you have a drift detection checker?
[16:01] Priya Nair: we have an ops agent that periodically validates firewall and egress rules against a declared policy. it can trigger alerts and auto-remediate if configured. we'll include the agent config in the runbook.
[16:17] Jordan Lee: jumping ahead to remediation — for the PoC we'll run the drift tests daily and do a controlled failover to validate containment steps.
[16:25] Marcus Vale: great. I want to call out network ops will ask for a dry-run where we test the deny-all list causes minimal service disruption. 
[16:34] Priya Nair: understood — that is part of week 1 in the PoC. we'll provide a test plan with expected outcomes and rollback steps.
[16:42] Sana Ortiz: one more: can labels and annotations be redacted from logs? we sometimes have internal project names that are sensitive.
[16:50] Priya Nair: yes, we have redaction rules and can mask or tokenise labels before emitting logs.
[16:57] Eli Chen: are there known issues with using HSM appliances behind NAT? some of our HSMs are on private VLANs that only allow inbound nexthop proxy.
[17:06] Priya Nair: as long as the runtime can establish mutual TLS to the HSM endpoint, connectivity via NAT is fine. if you have inbound-only constraints, we may need to deploy a small gateway in a DMZ that proxies requests to the HSM. we can advise on that architecture.
[17:24] Jordan Lee: OK folks — last 10 minutes let's cover handoff and concrete deliverables. Priya will produce runbook + snippets and Jordan will send compliance artifacts. Marcus to confirm schedule for PoC. Eli to draft auditor questions and Sana to gather KMS details.
[17:41] Marcus Vale: I'll confirm PoC resources and get back by Friday.
[17:45] Eli Chen: I'll compile a prioritized auditor checklist and share it with Jordan.
[17:49] Sana Ortiz: I'll export our current firewall rules and the list of allowed endpoints and drop them into the shared drive.
[17:55] Jordan Lee: great. I'm capturing next steps in the chat and will email the artifacts. Anything else?
[18:02] Marcus Vale: one more quick question — fallback behavior: if the control plane can't talk to the runtime during a maintenance window, do in-flight requests fail open or closed?
[18:12] Priya Nair: fail closed for management ops but inference continues as usual for in-flight sessions — the runtime keeps serving from the local model cache. management operations (deploy, update) will be queued until the control plane reconnects.
[18:28] Eli Chen: cool. fine by us.
[18:30] Jordan Lee: thanks everyone. we'll circle back after we share artifacts and schedule the PoC kickoff.
[18:36] Marcus Vale: thanks all.
[18:37] meeting end notes: items captured in next_steps/action_items above. attachments promised: SOC2/ISO PDFs, NACL/iptables examples, eBPF snippet, audit log schema, PoC plan.

Transcript notes: transcription contains occasional mis-hears (e.g., K V cache vs KV cache), and a few speaker label swaps early on. timestamps are approximate and inserted every ~15-60s.
